items.title: The Minkowski affine four-space: the form $\eta$, causal cones, frames and Lorentz maps
items.statement:
With $\mathbb R^4$ the space of functions $4\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-function-space]]) put $V:=\mathbb R^4$, and let $A$ be the set $\mathbb R^4$ together with the map $V\times A\to A$, $(v,p)\mapsto v+p$, given by function addition; then $(v+v')+p=v+(v'+p)$, $0+p=p$, and for all $p,q\in A$ there is exactly one $v\in V$ with $v+p=q$ ([[def-vector-space]]), so $A$ is an affine space with translation space $V$. Fix the ordered basis $e_0,\dots,e_3$ with $e_a(b):=1$ for $b=a$ and $0$ otherwise, and write $v=v^0e_0+\dots+v^3e_3$ ([[def-linear-basis]], [[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]). The **Minkowski form** is $\eta(v,w):=-v^0w^0+v^1w^1+v^2w^2+v^3w^3$; it is the standard bilinear form of [[def-standard-bilinear-form-on-a-coordinate-space]] with the sign of the first coordinate reversed and the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] on the last three coordinates, so it is a symmetric bilinear form ([[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]]) whose matrix in $(e_0,\dots,e_3)$ is $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$; that matrix is invertible, so $\eta$ is nondegenerate ([[def-matrix-radicals-rank-and-nondegeneracy-of-a-bilinear-form]]). A vector $v\ne0$ is **timelike** when $\eta(v,v)<0$, **null** when $\eta(v,v)=0$ and **spacelike** when $\eta(v,v)>0$; it is **causal** when $\eta(v,v)\le0$, and then $v^0\ne0$, so it is **future-directed** when $v^0>0$ and **past-directed** when $v^0<0$ ([[def-real-order]]). Put $C^+:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)\le0,\ v^0>0\}$ for the **future causal cone**. The **standard orientation** of $V$ is the orientation class of $(e_0,\dots,e_3)$ ([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]). A **Lorentz map** is an invertible linear $L:V\to V$ ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]) with $\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)$ for all $v,w\in V$; in the basis above this is exactly $M^{\mathsf T}\eta M=\eta$, where $M=[L]_{(e_0,\dots,e_3)}$, $\eta$ also denotes $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ and the matrix transpose is [[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]], by [[thm-change-of-basis-for-a-bilinear-form-is-congruence]] (a linear map preserving $\eta$ is automatically invertible because $\eta$ is nondegenerate). $L$ is **proper** when $\det L=1$ ([[def-determinant-of-a-linear-operator]]) and **orthochronous** when $L(C^+)=C^+$; a **frame** of $A$ is a point $o\in A$ with an ordered basis $(u_0,\dots,u_3)$ of $V$ satisfying $\eta(u_a,u_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ and $u_0\in C^+$, and the **coordinates** of $p\in A$ in that frame are the unique $(x^0,\dots,x^3)$ with $p=o+x^0u_0+\dots+x^3u_3$. For nonnegative integers $p,q$, a **tensor of type
$(p,q)$** on $V$ is a map $(V^*)^p\times V^q\to\mathbb R$ that is linear in
each argument separately, where $V^*$ is the algebraic dual of
[[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]]. An empty product is a singleton,
so a $(0,0)$ tensor is a scalar. Covectors are the $(0,1)$ case, a vector $v$
defines the $(1,0)$ tensor $\theta\mapsto\theta(v)$, and a **two-form** is a
skew-symmetric $(0,2)$ tensor. These objects are maps, with arrays recording
their components in a chosen basis.

Fix a frame $(o,(u_a))$ and define its linear coordinate map
$B:\mathbb R^4\to V$ by $B\xi:=\sum_a\xi^au_a$. It is invertible because
$(u_a)$ is a basis, and $\eta(B\xi,B\zeta)=\eta(\xi,\zeta)$ by its defining
pairings. For a Lorentz map $L:V\to V$, put $N:=[L]_{(u_a)}$, identifying
its matrix with the linear map $B^{-1}LB$ on $\mathbb R^4$. With origin fixed
and new basis $u'_a:=L^{-1}u_a$, the coordinates of the same point obey
$x'=Nx$: indeed $p-o=Bx=L^{-1}Bx'$ is equivalent to this identity.
The basis is orthonormal since $L^{-1}$ preserves $\eta$, and it is a frame
when $L$ is orthochronous, since then $L^{-1}u_0\in C^+$.

For a fixed vector $v$, covector $\theta$ and two-form $F$, let
$\widehat v:=B^{-1}v$, $\widehat\theta_a:=\theta(u_a)$ and
$\widehat F_{ab}:=F(u_a,u_b)$ be their old component columns and matrix;
primes denote the corresponding components in $(u'_a)$. Then

$$\widehat v'=N\widehat v,\qquad \widehat\theta'=(N^{-1})^{\mathsf T}\widehat\theta,\qquad \widehat F'=(N^{-1})^{\mathsf T}\widehat F N^{-1}.$$

The vector law follows from $B'=L^{-1}B=BN^{-1}$. Substituting
$u'_a=\sum_bu_b(N^{-1})^b{}_a$ into $\theta(u'_a)$ and $F(u'_a,u'_b)$ gives
the other two laws by linearity and bilinearity. Equivalently, the coordinate
functional $\theta\circ B'$ is $(\theta\circ B)\circ N^{-1}$, the transpose
operation of [[def-transpose-of-a-linear-map]], and the coordinate bilinear
form obeys $F(B'\xi,B'\zeta)=F(BN^{-1}\xi,BN^{-1}\zeta)$. The geometric
objects themselves are unchanged. In the standard frame $B=\operatorname{id}$,
$N$ is the standard coordinate matrix of $L$; in a general frame it is
$B^{-1}LB$. Finally, a fixed positive real $c$ is separate extra structure: the coordinate $x^0$ has the dimension of length and the time coordinate is $t:=x^0/c$.
items.strategy: Direct definition with the elementary verifications recorded where they belong to the definition: bilinearity and symmetry of $\eta$ from its coordinate formula, nondegeneracy from the invertible matrix $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, the implication $\eta(v,v)\le0$ and $v\ne0$ $\Rightarrow$ $v^0\ne0$ from $v^0^2\ge v^1^2+v^2^2+v^3^2$, and the matrix form $\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)\iff M^{\mathsf T}\eta M=\eta$ from the congruence law for the matrix of a bilinear form under a change of basis. No physical claim is made; identifying $A$ with physical spacetime and $c$ with the speed of light in vacuum is a later physical premise.

references.title: David Tong, Dynamics and Relativity, University of Cambridge Part IA Mathematical Tripos (Lent 2013), §7.1–§7.4.7, printed pp. 107–145
Sean M. Carroll, Lecture Notes on General Relativity (arXiv:gr-qc/9712019v1), Chapter 1, printed pp. 1–30

items.title: The explicit Lorentz boost preserves $\eta$, has determinant $1$ and preserves the future cone
items.statement: Let $0\le\beta<1$ and put $\gamma:=(1-\beta^2)^{-1/2}>0$ ([[def-rational-power]], [[lem-rational-power-laws]]). Define $\Lambda_\beta:V\to V$ by $(\Lambda_\beta v)_0=\gamma(v_0-\beta v_1)$, $(\Lambda_\beta v)_1=\gamma(v_1-\beta v_0)$, $(\Lambda_\beta v)_2=v_2$, $(\Lambda_\beta v)_3=v_3$. Then $\Lambda_\beta$ is linear ([[def-linear-map]]), $\Lambda_\beta$ is a proper orthochronous Lorentz map, and more precisely: (a) $\eta(\Lambda_\beta v,\Lambda_\beta w)=\eta(v,w)$ for all $v,w\in V$; (b) $\det\Lambda_\beta=1$; (c) $\Lambda_\beta(C^+)=C^+$; (d) $\Lambda_\beta^{-1}=\Lambda_{-\beta}$. In particular a future causal vector has future causal image and $\eta(\Lambda_\beta v,\Lambda_\beta v)=\eta(v,v)$ for every $v$ ([[def-real-order]], [[lem-of-square-monotone]]). The hypothesis $0\le\beta<1$ is not removable: at $\beta=1$ the factor $\gamma$ is undefined.
items.strategy: Substitution in the coordinate formula of $\eta$ gives $-\gamma^2(v_0-\beta v_1)^2+\gamma^2(v_1-\beta v_0)^2=\gamma^2(1-\beta^2)(-v_0^2+v_1^2)$ with the last two coordinates unchanged, and $\gamma^2(1-\beta^2)=1$; the $0$–$1$ block of the matrix has determinant $\gamma^2(1-\beta^2)=1$ and the remaining block is the identity, giving $\det\Lambda_\beta=1$; for future causal $v$ one has $|v_1|\le\sqrt{v_1^2+v_2^2+v_3^2}\le v_0$ from $\eta(v,v)\le0$, and $0\le\beta<1$ gives $(\Lambda_\beta v)_0=\gamma(v_0-\beta v_1)\ge\gamma(1-\beta)v_0>0$, so $\Lambda_\beta(C^+)\subseteq C^+$; applying the same argument to $\Lambda_{-\beta}$ and using $\Lambda_\beta\Lambda_{-\beta}=\mathrm{id}$ (again $\gamma^2(1-\beta^2)=1$) gives equality. No empirical relativity principle is proved.

items.title: Proper time along a $C^1$ future timelike curve: strictly increasing reparametrization with $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$
items.statement: Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval ([[def-interval]]) and let $z:J\to\mathbb R^4$ be of class $C^1$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) with $\eta(z'(s),z'(s))<0$ and $z^0{}'(s)>0$ for every $s\in J$; $z'$ is the derivative of the vector-valued curve ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]) and such a $z$ is called a $C^1$ future timelike curve. Put $g(s):=-\eta(z'(s),z'(s))>0$, fix $s_0\in J$, and define $\tau(s):=c^{-1}\int_{s_0}^{s}\sqrt{g(u)}\,du$ for $s\in J$. Then: (1) $g$ is continuous on $J$ and so is $s\mapsto\sqrt{g(s)}$, where $\sqrt{\cdot}$ is the nonnegative square root ([[thm-of-square-roots]], [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], [[thm-composition-of-continuous-functions]]); (2) $\tau$ is differentiable on $J$ with $\tau'(s)=c^{-1}\sqrt{g(s)}>0$, hence $\tau$ is strictly increasing on $J$, injective, and continuous ([[cor-primitives-of-a-continuous-function]], [[thm-monotonicity-from-the-derivative]]); (3) the inverse $\tau^{-1}:\tau[J]\to J$ is differentiable at every point $\tau(s)$ of the interval $\tau[J]$, with $(\tau^{-1})'(\tau(s))=c/\sqrt{g(s)}$ ([[thm-continuous-inverse]], [[thm-derivative-of-an-inverse]]); (4) the reparametrized curve $z\circ\tau^{-1}:\tau[J]\to\mathbb R^4$ is differentiable at every $\tau(s)$, with tangent $U(\tau(s)):=c\,z'(s)/\sqrt{g(s)}$ satisfying $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ ([[thm-chain-rule]], [[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]]); (5) if instead $\eta(z'(s),z'(s))=0$ for all $s\in J$, then $g=0$, $\tau\equiv0$ on $J$ and $\tau$ is not injective, so a null curve carries no proper-time parametrization ([[cor-zero-derivative-implies-constant]]); (6) if $z(s)=p+sv$ with $\eta(v,v)<0$ and $v_0>0$, then $\tau(s)=c^{-1}\sqrt{-\eta(v,v)}\,(s-s_0)$ and $U=c\,v/\sqrt{-\eta(v,v)}$ is constant ([[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]], [[def-derivative]]). The identification of such straight lines with inertial motion is a physical premise and is not asserted here.
items.strategy: $C^1$ gives continuity of the components $z^a{}'$ and [[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]] passes between the vector-valued and component statements; the four squares $(z^a{}')^2$ and their signed sum are continuous by [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $g$ is continuous; $\sqrt g$ is continuous because squaring is a continuous injection of $[0,\infty)$ onto itself with continuous inverse $\sqrt{\cdot}$ ([[lem-of-square-monotone]], [[thm-continuous-inverse]]), and composition preserves continuity. [[cor-primitives-of-a-continuous-function]] makes $\tau$ a primitive of the continuous function $c^{-1}\sqrt g$ on $J$, giving (2) with [[thm-monotonicity-from-the-derivative]]; [[thm-derivative-of-an-inverse]] (hypotheses: $\tau$ continuous and injective on the interval $J$, $\tau'(s)\ne0$) gives (3); [[thm-chain-rule]] applied to the components of $z\circ\tau^{-1}$ and reassembled gives (4), where $\eta(U,U)=(c^2/g)\eta(z',z')=-c^2$ uses bilinearity and symmetry of $\eta$; (5) is the zero integrand case; (6) is direct computation with constant $z'=v$.

items.title: Antisymmetric contractions vanish and $mU'=q\Phi(U)$ preserves $\eta(U,U)$
items.statement:
Let $(V,\eta)$ be the four-dimensional real Minkowski vector space of [[def-em-minkowski-affine-space]], with the fixed form of signature $(-1,1,1,1)$. Let $F:V	imes V	o\mathbb R$ be a skew-symmetric bilinear form, $F(u,v)=-F(v,u)$ for all $u,v\in V$ ([[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]]). Since $\eta$ is nondegenerate, for each $u\in V$ there is exactly one $\Phi(u)\in V$ with $\eta(\Phi(u),w)=F(w,u)$ for all $w\in V$ ([[thm-bilinear-forms-correspond-to-linear-maps-into-the-dual]], [[def-matrix-radicals-rank-and-nondegeneracy-of-a-bilinear-form]]), and $\Phi:V	o V$ is linear ([[def-linear-map]]); with $F_{\alpha eta}:=F(e_\alpha,e_ eta)$ in a frame $\Phi(u)^\mu=\eta^{\mu\alpha}F_{\alpha eta}u^ eta$, the index-raised form of $F$. Then $\eta(u,\Phi(u))=0$ for every $u\in V$; in components $u_\mu F^\mu{}_
u u^
u=0$. Consequently, if $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a nonempty open interval ([[def-interval]]), $U:J	o V$ is differentiable ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and $m\,U'(s)=q\,\Phi(U(s))$ on $J$ for some real $m
e0$ and $q$, then $s\mapsto\eta(U(s),U(s))$ is constant on $J$ ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]], [[cor-zero-derivative-implies-constant]]). The same norm-conservation conclusion holds for a family of skew forms $F_s$ and their pointwise operators $\Phi_s$ defined by $\eta(\Phi_s(u),w)=F_s(w,u)$, when $mU'(s)=q\Phi_s(U(s))$: no derivative of $F_s$ is required. In particular one may evaluate a varying field $F_x$ along a differentiable trajectory $x(s)$. This is a conditional statement about the given equation; it does not assert that this equation governs any particle.
items.strategy: For each $u$, $w\mapsto F(w,u)$ is a linear functional. The nondegenerate finite-dimensional form $\eta$ identifies $V$ with $V^*$, so it gives a unique $\Phi(u)$; bilinearity and uniqueness make $\Phi$ linear. In a frame, evaluating the defining pairing at $w=e_\alpha$ gives $\eta_{\alpha\mu}\Phi(u)^\mu=F_{\alpha\beta}u^\beta$, hence $\Phi(u)^\mu=\eta^{\mu\alpha}F_{\alpha\beta}u^\beta$. Taking $w=u$ gives $\eta(\Phi(u),u)=F(u,u)=0$ by skew-symmetry, and symmetry of $\eta$ gives $\eta(u,\Phi(u))=0$. For the norm claim $f(s):=\eta(U(s),U(s))=\sum_a\epsilon_a(U^a(s))^2$, with $\epsilon=(-1,1,1,1)$, satisfies $f'=2\eta(U,U')$ by the product rule. The equation gives $\eta(U,U')=(q/m)\eta(U,\Phi(U))=0$, so the zero-derivative theorem on the open interval $J$ makes $f$ constant. The identical pointwise calculation with $\Phi_s$ proves the varying-form clause: differentiate $\eta(U,U)$ only, not $F_s$ or $\Phi_s$. No constant-field assumption is used in that clause.

items.title: Explicit mathematical hypothesis/convention examples
items.statement:
With $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$: (i) the vector $v$ with components
$(1,0,0,0)$ is future timelike and unit, $\eta(v,v)=-1$. (ii) For $0<\beta<1$
the boost $\Lambda_\beta$ of
[[lem-em-boost-preserves-metric]] sends $v$ to the vector with components
$(\gamma,-\gamma\beta,0,0)$,
whose quadratic value $\eta(\Lambda_\beta v,\Lambda_\beta v)$ is
$-\gamma^2(1-\beta^2)=-1$ and whose time component
$\gamma$ is positive; at $\beta=1$ the factor $\gamma$ is undefined, so the
hypothesis $0\le\beta<1$ cannot be dropped. (iii) The null line
$z(s)=(s,s,0,0)$, $s\in\mathbb R$, has $\eta(z',z')=0$, so the proper-time
construction of [[lem-em-proper-time-reparametrization]] gives $\tau\equiv0$,
which is not an invertible parameter: the timelike hypothesis cannot be weakened
to causal. (iv) For the symmetric nonzero form $F:=\eta$ one has
$\Phi=\mathrm{id}$ and $\eta(v,\Phi(v))=\eta(v,v)=-1\ne0$, so the antisymmetry
hypothesis of [[lem-em-antisymmetric-tensor-contraction]] is genuine. (v) For
the skew form with $F_{01}=1$, $F_{10}=-1$ and other coefficients zero, the
operator of [[lem-em-antisymmetric-tensor-contraction]] sends $e_0$ to $-e_1$:
$\eta(-e_1,w)=-w^1=F(w,e_0)$. Thus its invariant pairing and standard
raised-index formula have the same sign, and $\eta(e_0,\Phi(e_0))=0$. No
physical clock premise or experimental claim is used.
items.strategy: Five direct computations in the fixed standard frame: evaluation of $\eta$ on the given vectors, substitution of $v$ in the boost formula, the vanishing of the null tangent, and the identification $\Phi=\mathrm{id}$ when $F=\eta$ (uniqueness in the defining property of $\Phi$). For (v), the first column of $\eta^{-1}F$ is $(0,-1,0,0)$; both pairings equal $-w^1$, and the time-space orthogonality is immediate. All are exact finite computations; no source or physical assumption is needed.
